nameStory: Sea Hair gets its name from its resemblance to long, green hair floating in the water. The scientific name Chaetomorpha comes from Greek words meaning 'bristle form,' perfectly describing these thread-like algae that sway back and forth with ocean currents like underwater locks.
description: Sea Hair is a green marine algae that looks exactly like its name suggests - long, thin strands of bright green 'hair' growing underwater. Each strand is unbranched and can grow several inches long, creating dense mats or tufts that attach to rocks, shells, or other hard surfaces in shallow coastal waters. Unlike land plants, this is actually made up of long chains of individual cells lined up end to end, creating these distinctive thread-like structures. You'll typically find it in tide pools and shallow waters along rocky shores.

idTips.label: Thread-like form
idTips.description: Long, unbranched green strands that feel slippery and somewhat coarse when wet, like wet fishing line or coarse thread

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Vibrant emerald to grass-green color that stays bright even when wet, much more vivid than most seaweeds

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms dense tufts or mats attached to hard surfaces, with individual strands radiating outward like a green pom-pom

idTips.label: Texture when handled
idTips.description: Feels slippery but slightly rough to the touch, not slimy like some seaweeds, and individual strands can be separated easily

idTips.label: Marine habitat
idTips.description: Always found in saltwater environments, never in freshwater, typically in areas that get regular wave action

habitat: Sea Hair thrives in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools, on wave-exposed rocks, and attached to shells or other hard surfaces in the intertidal zone. You'll find it from Maine to Connecticut wherever there are rocky shores with good water circulation. It prefers areas that get regular wave action but can also grow in quieter bays and harbors on pier pilings or jetties.

seasonality.spring: Growth begins to pick up as water temperatures rise, with new bright green growth appearing on established patches.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most abundant and visible growth, forming dense mats in tide pools and shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing but may begin to show some browning or die-back as temperatures start to cool.
seasonality.winter: Growth slows significantly in cold water, and many patches may die back or become less prominent until spring.

funFact: Each 'hair' strand is actually a single, incredibly long cell - one of the largest single cells you can see with the naked eye, sometimes containing thousands of individual nuclei all working together in one continuous tube!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other thread-like green algae, but Sea Hair's unbranched, coarse texture and bright green color help distinguish it. Remember: if it looks like green hair underwater and feels rough rather than slimy, you've probably found Sea Hair.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'algae,' this is quite different from the slimy green algae you might see in freshwater ponds - marine algae like Sea Hair are much more structured and often serve as important habitat for small marine creatures.
compareHints: Sea Hair differs from its relatives in the Chaetomorpha genus by its specific thread-like, unbranched form and relatively coarse texture. Other species in this genus may have different branching patterns or cell arrangements, but Sea Hair maintains its simple, hair-like structure throughout its growth. It's generally more robust and easier to handle than some of its more delicate relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Sea Hair (Chaetomorpha linum), this species has noticeably thicker, coarser filaments and tends toward darker green coloration.
Compared to the much more common Sea Hair (Chaetomorpha linum), this species has slightly thicker, more rigid filaments and tends to form denser mats.

**Note: Limited comparative data available** Compared to Sea Hair (Chaetomorpha linum), this species may have different cell dimensions and strand characteristics, but distinguishing between Chaetomorpha species typically requires microscopic measurement of cell size and other technical features.
